title: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim
subtitle: Command of Evidence · 17 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **17 of the official questions in Command of Evidence are this one** — 2 Easy, 8 Medium, 7 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question asks which quotation from a scholar, a survey respondent, a critic or an article would best support or illustrate someone's claim or conclusion.
- The choices are quotations in the voice of an outside commentator, not lines from a literary work.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Pin down the precise claim, including any qualifier such as 'unifying several traditions', 'between volunteers and non-volunteers', or 'imagined rather than precise'.
- 2) Treat each quotation as a piece of evidence and ask whether it shows that precise relationship.
- 3) Choose the one that matches the qualifier, not just the subject.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: Every choice is about the right subject, but only one captures the specific relationship in the claim.
You pick a quotation that praises or describes the subject vividly without showing the particular point, such as connections among the wrong group or a single tradition instead of several.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
